e1-emuA:
There has been a lot of changes in the legality and regulations of psychedelics, and a lot of those changes haven’t quite made it into the literature most communities are familiar with yet. In the US, Oregon is set to start opening licensed psilocybin service centers in 2023. Colorado has created a regulated natural medicine system, set to begin licensing in 2025. New Mexico has passed a Medical Psilocybin Act, set to take effect in 2025. In Australia, psychiatrists have been able to use psilocybin and MDMA (among a limited set of conditions) since 2023.

It's not all roses, either. In 2024, the FDA issued a "Complete Response Letter" for the submitted MDMA application, asking for more evidence in order to be considered for approval. Portugal is often spoken about as a place where "they've legalized everything" -- which is false! They've decriminalized small amounts of all drugs for personal possession and use, but trafficking is still criminal.
e1-emuB:
A great deal of literature coming out of the psychedelic communities has been slow to recognize how quickly psychedelics are being legalized and regulated for human use. In the United States, licensed psilocybin service centers are starting to open in Oregon (2023), a regulated system has been set up and licensing started in Colorado (2025) for “natural medicine”, and New Mexico recently passed the Medical Psilocybin Act (2025). Outside of the US, certain psychiatrists can now prescribe psilocybin and MDMA to a limited number of patients for certain conditions (2023) in Australia.

The legalization train has not been a smooth ride. The FDA recently released a Complete Response Letter (CRL) asking for more evidence before allowing the submitted application of MDMA (2024). And the reality in Portugal is not that all psychedelic substances have been legalized (a common lazy claim), but rather that small amounts of all drugs have been decriminalized for personal use while trafficking still remains criminal.
e10-emuA:
The practicalities of safety and support are what matter, what needs to be addressed with care and attention, in preparing for, nourishing, screening for appropriate interaction, dosing, and what to do in case of emergency, etc. A lot of this is now covered in the Altered States Triage material I’m currently using.

Legal issues differ greatly, and often are not well defined, but some basic understanding of what is or is not allowed in a given community, what needs to be private, what might be insurable or require legal review, etc. is valuable to have in writing. “I don’t think anybody here has ever heard of that,” is not the same as a legal opinion.
e10-emuB:
A whole slew of other supports would be helpful. Details on preparing for a ceremony, nutrition, how to screen for who should/shouldn’t be interacting with the entity, what to do if someone takes too high of a dose, etc… Most of this information can be found on my Altered States Triage page here .

If what I’m doing is illegal in my area, how can I know for sure? It’s hard to know in some areas, because the laws are not always spelled out clearly. It would be best to have this spelled out in writing somewhere, so that people know exactly what they can do, what they can’t do, what might be considered private acts, what can be covered by insurance, etc… A good place to start might be by asking if anybody in the community has heard of it being done before.
e11-emuA:
One of the things that many people seem to be called to do after an intensely psychedelic or mystical experience is to “find their tribe,” “settle down in a village,” or to otherwise assist others to “get where they’ve been.”

I understand this call. I also understand that it can come with an inflated sense of self. You come back from this experience and you believe you can fix everyone with your love and soon find that there are people who don’t want to be fixed and those who want to but yet live lives contrary to that change and those that need more help than you imagined.

So while I also understand this call, I think it’s important to not be inflaed with a sense of omnipotence when living this calling out.
e11-emuB:
One of the great impulses that people feel following a deep psychedelic or mystical experience is the urge to find one’s tribe, to form a village, to help others access the experience.

I know this feeling very well. I also know that this feeling often comes mixed with a feeling of omnipotence. It is easy when you come back from such an experience to think you can fix anyone with love, but all it takes is a few run-ins with people who do not want to fix themselves, or who want to but can’t stop shooting themselves in the foot, or who have way bigger problems than you ever imagined, to deflate this feeling.

The call is real, but building a village on a foundation of omnipotence is a bad idea.
e12-emuA:
The need for the sections on capacity and on membership, later on in this article, is because many groups have begun in a kind of collective spiritual euphoria, and immediately begun recruiting, not realizing how quickly things can get out of hand arithmetically!

And the next wave is useful, because when the initial euphoria wears off and the call becomes a bit more sober, the community can be a launching pad for the next phase of spiritual training, and eventually a call to go out and start a new experiment. That's one answer to the charge that spiritual communities are essentially a way for people with some privilege to escape from the world!
e12-emuB:
The reason for setting capacity and defining membership, both covered later in this article, is to avoid the temptation to take on too many people, too quickly, which sometimes happens in the first flush of collective spiritual euphoria.

Once the initial flush of euphoria has passed, the call may still prove useful as a training ground for people to move on from. This partly answers the objection that forming a commune is a privileged way of escaping from society.
e2-emuA:
To be sure, the legality of this varies depending on country, state, substance, religious status, what exactly one does, and so on, and if one is going to build a community around this one should definitely get actual legal advice in the area.

And even where it is legal, most of the intentional communities I know that are using psychedelics prefer not to talk about it, for fear of scaring off potential parents, neighbors, insurance, official types, and so on.

I am doing so for this model because I felt it would not be an honest model to not talk about this, and because a good many of the people reading this are probably already familiar with my psychedelic-related writing, if not from the Rethinking Recovery posts here, then from my loveyhuasca writing on Haoma . And I wanted to be honest in this article about the good and the bad.
e2-emuB:
I would imagine there are many differences between the legal situations for various communities in different countries and states. It probably also varies by the specific substances that are used, whether the community is officially religious or not, and what else the community is doing. I can't cover that here. If someone is considering a particular community they will need to get actual legal advice.

Most communities that are using psychedelics don't advertise that fact, because even where the law might be on their side there may be issues with parents of children that they want to welcome to the community, or other neighbors, or insurance, or local authorities who may not understand the nuances of the law.

I'm talking about it here because not to talk about it would be to falsify my model. Many of the people who read this article are likely already familiar with my writing about psychedelics on loveyhuasca or Haoma . I want to be able to write an honest article, and that means talking about both the value and the risk.
e3-emuA:
It sounds like a lot to ask, but consider the negative case first: the results from the Global Ayahuasca Survey suggest that physical and mental adverse effects are quite common from ayahuasca use. Severe adverse effects are far less common, but again context is everything. The fundamental problem is that these medicines open things up faster than people (or communities) are often able to support them.

On top of that, these medicines seem to attract people who want to experience revelation more than they want to do the work that follows. While this isn’t true of everyone, there are certainly plenty of people who will happily go to a dozen ceremonies and learn six different origin stories, while never dealing with simple issues like apologizing when they’re wrong. If a community is set up to primarily facilitate a peak experience, this problem is only going to be exacerbated.

On the other hand, from my own experience, the communal aspect of using these medicines can be incredibly valuable. Psychedelics can be used to let go of the patterns that dominate most conversations, and can create powerful bonds between people. They can also be confusing, lead to grandiosity, create dependency, and lead to messy interactions with other people. Whether they do or not, in my experience, comes down to the maturity of the community that’s supporting their use.
e3-emuB:
One of the main reasons against is actually the results of the Global Ayahuasca Survey. Not so much those that severe physical and mental issues are common, they're not, but that having those at all is pretty common, and that it's highly contingent on context. I believe using these medicines opens material that often is too fast for someone (or a group) to deal with.

Also, these medicines tend to attract people who want all the revelation and none of the work. Communities that are trying to focus on the peak experience are not going to be effective.

On the other hand, having used these medicines communally myself, I've found them very helpful in releasing the problematic ways that I hold myself in conversation with others. They can bring people together in very strong ways, but also confuse, inflate, create dependency, and just be messy in general. It's all contingent on the maturity of the community around it.
e4-emuA:
It’s also about integration. When you gain insight and clarity about your life, you wake up and you’re still in the same environment you were in before it happened and no one knows what happened to you. This is where it can be super helpful to have gone through the experience in a community where people can be there for you and help you notice what happens to you in the months after.

It’s also that the deeper the experience, the more alienated you may feel after. When I had my original ayahuasca ego deaths at 26, I struggled to find people who had been there physically, even at Buddhist monasteries where enlightenment is preached! It’s also a time where you may feel a God/Savior complex (or maybe both at the same time? 😂) and you need to meet the right people to show you where you’re limited.

Finally, the people you’re relying on to support you, do you trust them? Your alternative is to pay people you don’t know to support you for a night. They may be great, but there’s also the possibility that the person stroking a feather over you only knows your for 4 hours and already has a cosmology they’re using to explain everything you say.
e4-emuB:
This is really excellent, I love that breakdown of the insights part. It’s one of the things that I think really needs a community to navigate. Even if you have great insight into yourself and your life, you’re going back into the same environment and no one knows what’s happened. Having people who can not only support you through the experience but also see the effects in the months after.

The deeper you go the more alienated you can feel. When I went through my first couple of ego deaths on ayahuasca I found it really hard to find people IRL who had had similar experiences. Even going to Buddhist monasteries who preach about enlightenment no one had been there (at the time I was 26). It can definitely lead to God / Savior complexes (I had both) but life will send you the right people to show you where you need to grow. 😂

This is another great point. You could buy that support from people you don’t know for a single night but it’s not the same as having people you know and trust. Sometimes the paid for support is really good but other times the guy tickling you with a feather has only known you for 4 hours and already has a whole cosmology to explain what’s happening to you.
e5-emuA:
For one, if you’re working within a community, your sober sitter may be someone who has known you for a long time. There’s a difference between being held and simply being watched—this is especially relevant when you’re working with medicines like iboga that require screening and watching for the duration of a long and potentially medically risky experience.

Second, your peers can help you reality-check your downloads. Psychedelics can be an incredible source of insight, but they can also be an incredible source of nonsense. It can be hard to tell the difference between the two since the lighting is the same. It helps to have friends who know you and your history well enough to offer a perspective on whether what you’re bringing back is insight or simply more of the same stuff you got from your mother.

Third, community helps provide a rhythm for medicine work. Many medicine traditions use community timing for their ceremonies, rather than allowing people to take medicine when they want. This can be extremely helpful for avoiding compulsive medicine-taking and for allowing integration time to happen.
e5-emuB:
Account Type: Free Membership Even if you're going sober, the sitter is likely to be someone in your community. Plus, it's different to just be watched vs held. Especially when taking something like iboga, which can last for quite some time and has medical risks, it's a good idea to be screened and watched the entire time.

2) Peer Reality Checking of Downloads Psychedelics have the capacity to create both real insight and convincing bullshit with no difference in lighting effects. Having friends around to help sift through your downloads who know your history can be really helpful to tell which is which (and what is just you talking about your mother again).

3) Communal Timing Many medicinal systems that use these substances do so in a communal setting with certain timings. By being part of a community that can help you time your ceremonies, it can be easier to avoid being compelled to keep taking them over and over again, giving you time to integrate.

It will be easier to deal with logistics when there’s more of ya. Having somebody that the collective trusts to watch the kids. Not having to drive away from the ceremony. Having people that can bring water, be close by and sit quietly with somebody as they re-integrate back into normal consiousness.

There will be people to play with! Raves are great because they allow people to skip to that part of intimacy where they feel close enough to do wild things together before they know enough about each other to truly trust each other. Imagine doing ecstatic music and dance with people in a community that ya do know… 💃🕺

Yeah, psychedelics are not for everybody. There will be people that shouldn’t do them. There will be communities that shouldn’t be doing them. Just like there are a lot of people that are hella stoked on psychedelics there will be casualties when people are not competent enough to work with these powerful substances. If a community is going to dive into this it needs to do so in a humble way. Knowing that sometimes the answer will be no, or not now, or go work with so-and-so, or I fucked that one up.
e6-emuB:
This will help make things a bit easier, there will be people there to watch the kids (collectively agreed upon people that are all trusted), so that no one has to drive away, someone will have brought water with them and will be close by, someone will be there to sit with to help return to normal consciousness, etc.

2. There will be people there to play with. Raves are amazing because they create the space for people to connect intimately way before they have built up trust, and this will be a way to bring that ecstatic music and movement into a community of people who already know each other. 💃🕺

It’s important to note that there are people that should not do psychedelics and communities that should not do psychedelics. There will be casualties of this just by the nature of the enthusiasm of people. Those who move in this direction as a community need to be humble about saying no, or pausing, or sending people somewhere else, as well as humble about admitting when something has gone wrong.
e7-emuA:
One of the things I want to make clear is that I don’t advocate for shaman, per se. In this, I know I disagree with many of the traditional lineages I have worked with (particularly in ayahuasca and Bwiti).

My issue is that often the “shaman” in these settings is a charismatic individual on the retreat circuit who may or may not be vetted by anybody, who may or may not be a sexual predator, who is financially motivated to get people to come back to them specifically, and who has little to be accountable to. When one is opening so deeply, this is a major concern.

I am not sure yet how to avoid this in a culture that works with medicine in a more peer-like fashion, as there will likely always be somebody that people gravitate towards and look up to. Rotating the “shaman” role and being accountable to one another may help, but I’m not sure it will be enough.
e7-emuB:
In particular, I don’t believe in “shamans.” This goes against the grain of a lot of traditional lineages. A lot of ayahuasca, Bwiti, and other lineages take a problem with this.

I fundamentally don’t like the idea of a charismatic leader. For instance, the idea of flying across the globe to sit at the feet of some potentially charismatic individual who’s popped up on the global retreat circuit. They may or may not be someone with wisdom, they may or may not have much vetting, they may or may not be sexually attracted to shitwomping people, they’re probably leveraging the experience as a paycheck, and they may or may not know what they’re talking about. When people are deeply opening themselves, I think this is a pretty dangerous combination.

One of the things I’m not sure how to navigate, though, in this peer-led way of working with medicine is how to avoid people becoming de facto shamans anyway. I suspect rotating roles and a deep commitment to holding one another accountable are good, but that they’re not enough.
e8-emuA:
I am teaching people to learn to do for themselves and each other, within appropriate scopes of competence. See here for more on peer-held ceremonies, and here for more on the best psychopath shaman I ever met.

This doesn’t mean that the ceremonies I lead are casual. People are screened for medical and psychiatric contraindications, and educated about medication contraindications and combinations, and an appropriate sober sitter is required. Guidelines are set for circumstances in which to seek professional care, even emergency care. In a sense the bar for basic competence is higher when authority is distributed rather than centralized.

In addition, I am cautious about medicines and protocols which I consider to be more destabilizing and medically burdensome, including some uses of ketamine, mdma, and bufo. See the above articles for more explanation.
e8-emuB:
I do, however, advocate for people to learn how to guide each other, take care of each other, and to know when it’s beyond their competence. I talk a bit more about this in the piece on peer held ceremonies here and in the piece on the best psychopath shaman I’ve ever met here.

There’s a difference, though, between peer led and doing it casually. There needs to be screening, awareness of medical and psychiatric contraindications, knowledge of medication and medication combinations, an appropriate sober sitter present, and a clear idea of when to bring in professional help or go to the ER. When authority is distributed, it does not lower the bar of required competence.

Some of the medicines and protocols, such as some ketamine protocols, some MDMA work, and bufo, can be more destabilizing and medically burdensome. I talk more about that here.
e9-emuA:
For now, medicine will come after the other pl/ork. Reparenting, somatic capacity, peer counseling, etc. can’t be replaced by pharmacology.

Also, this helps weed out the ‘experience collectors’. If someone is unwilling to invest the time in relationship building (6months is not that long), why would they suddenly become more mature in that area because of visions?

Lastly, integration is a part of day to day life. Ceremony is a part of that, but the weeks that follow are where the real work is done. How are relationships? How are they living their life now? Sleep? Etc.
e9-emuB:
The reason for this is that the medicine will be behind the other pl/ork that is being done, and if a person doesn’t do the reparenting /somatic work/capacities work/peer counseling, etc. prior to the ceremony the medicine cannot do this work for them. The medicine can support one’s work, but it cannot create this work.

The second reason for this requirement is that it weeds out the experience collectors. If someone is not willing to do six months of this work it is a good sign that they will not make the inner shift toward more relational maturity simply because the visions they saw were cool.

A third reason is that integration is all about how a person lives their life after the ceremony.
